Timeline::searchsorted_left¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signatures¶

Timeline::searchsorted_left(const Timeline& values) -> Series
Timeline::searchsorted_right(const Timeline& values) -> Series
Timeline::to_epoch_nanos_flat() -> std::vector<std::int64_t>

This page covers the ordered insertion and raw tick-export family.

What These Methods Do¶

searchsorted_left(...) and searchsorted_right(...) answer the question: “if I inserted these query timestamps into this already-sorted timeline, at what positions would they land?”

That makes them useful for:

  • ordered lookup preparation

  • bin-edge reasoning

  • merge/as-of style temporal alignment

  • converting exact-or-nearest timestamp reasoning into integer positions

to_epoch_nanos_flat() is the low-level export surface that exposes the raw epoch-nanosecond representation as a flat integer vector.

Parameters¶

values

The timestamps whose insertion positions you want to compute.

The shape does not need to match the source timeline length; the result length matches the number of query timestamps you provide.

The behavioral toggle is the side rule:

  • searchsorted_left(...) Insert before existing equal timestamps.

  • searchsorted_right(...) Insert after existing equal timestamps.

That difference only matters when the query timestamp is already present.

Returns¶

Series Integer insertion positions for the search methods.

std::vector<std::int64_t> Raw epoch-nanosecond ticks for to_epoch_nanos_flat().

Notes¶

  • The search methods are meant for sorted 1D timelines.

  • Left versus right matters exactly at equal-key boundaries.

  • to_epoch_nanos_flat() is intentionally lower level: use it when you need to interoperate with external systems or numerical kernels that expect raw tick values instead of Timeline.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute left insertion positions for queries that land before, inside, and after the sorted range.

auto pos = sorted.searchsorted_left(queries);
std::cout << pluss::series::print(pos) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 2, 4]

Example 2. Switch to right insertion positions so equal timestamps fall after existing matches.

auto pos = sorted.searchsorted_right(queries);
std::cout << pluss::series::print(pos) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 4, 4]

Example 3. See the equal-key difference directly on timestamps that already exist in the sorted timeline.

auto left = sorted.searchsorted_left(pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-11-01T09:00:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T11:00:00Z",
}));
std::cout << pluss::series::print(left) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 2]

Example 4. Use the right-side rule on the same exact matches.

auto right = sorted.searchsorted_right(pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-11-01T09:00:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T11:00:00Z",
}));
std::cout << pluss::series::print(right) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 4]

Example 5. Export the same timeline as raw epoch nanoseconds.

auto ticks = base.to_epoch_nanos_flat();
std::cout << "[";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < ticks.size(); ++i) {
    if (i != 0) std::cout << ", ";
    std::cout << ticks[i];
}
std::cout << "]\n";

Output¶

[1730451600000000000, 1730456130000000000, 1735689599000000000, 1735689600000000000]
